text:
# Growing tomatoes in containers

Tomatoes grow well in pots on a balcony or patio, as long as they get at least six hours of direct sun a day. Choose a container that holds twenty litres or more, because a small pot dries out within hours on a warm afternoon and the plant stops setting fruit.

Fill the pot with a peat-free compost mixed with a handful of grit for drainage. Plant the seedling deeper than it sat in its nursery pot: the buried stem grows extra roots and makes the plant sturdier. Push a cane in beside it on the same day, so you do not damage the roots later.

Water deeply and regularly. Irregular watering, a soak after the compost has dried out completely, is the usual cause of split fruit and of the dark, sunken patches known as blossom end rot. In midsummer a large plant may need watering every morning and again in the evening.

Once the first flowers open, feed every week with a liquid fertiliser that is high in potash. Pinch out the side shoots that form between the main stem and the leaf stalks of cordon varieties, and tie the stem to its cane as it grows. Bush varieties need no pinching.

When the plant has set four or five trusses of fruit, pinch out the growing tip so the plant puts its energy into ripening what it already carries. Pick the tomatoes when they are fully coloured and slightly soft. Green fruit left at the end of the season will ripen indoors on a sunny windowsill or in a drawer next to a banana.
title: Growing tomatoes in containers

text:
# Opening principles for beginners

The first dozen moves of a chess game decide how comfortable the middle game will be. You do not need to memorise long sequences to play the opening well; a few principles cover most positions.

Control the centre. Pawns and pieces on the four central squares restrict the opponent's pieces and give your own the most room. Opening with the king's pawn or the queen's pawn two squares forward is popular for exactly this reason.

Develop your knights and bishops before you move any piece twice. A knight on its starting square controls only two or three squares, while a knight in the centre controls eight. Bring out the minor pieces towards the centre, usually knights before bishops, because the best square for a knight is clear earlier.

Castle early. Castling tucks the king behind a wall of pawns and connects the rooks, which can then move to open files. A king left in the centre after the pawns in front of it have moved is easy to attack.

Do not bring the queen out too soon. The queen is the most valuable piece, so the opponent can chase it with minor pieces and develop them at the same time, gaining tempo with every move.

Finally, think about what your opponent's last move threatens before you make your own. Many games between beginners are decided not by a deep plan but by a piece left undefended in the first ten moves.
title: Opening principles for beginners

text:
# Building a monthly household budget

A budget is a plan for the money you expect to receive in a month and where each part of it will go. Writing it down turns vague worries about spending into decisions you can actually make.

Start with income after tax: salaries, benefits and any regular side earnings. If your income varies from month to month, use the lowest month of the past year as your baseline, so a good month becomes a bonus rather than the plan.

Next, list fixed costs that are the same every month: rent or mortgage, council tax, insurance, phone contracts and loan repayments. Then estimate variable essentials such as groceries, energy and travel by looking at the last three months of bank statements and taking an average.

What remains is for savings and for everything else. Many people pay themselves first: a fixed transfer into a savings account on the day the salary arrives, before there is a chance to spend it. An emergency fund that covers three months of essential costs is a common first goal.

Track spending against the plan during the month, either with a spreadsheet, a notebook or a banking app that groups transactions by type. At the end of the month compare what happened with what you planned, adjust the categories that were unrealistic and carry on. A budget that is revised every month is far more useful than a perfect one that is abandoned after a few weeks.
title: Building a monthly household budget

text:
# Laying out a page with CSS flexbox

Flexbox is a CSS layout model for arranging items in a single row or column. You turn an element into a flex container with `display: flex`, and its direct children become flex items that the browser sizes and positions along the container's main axis.

The `flex-direction` property chooses that axis: `row`, the default, places items from left to right in a left-to-right language, and `column` stacks them from top to bottom. The cross axis runs at right angles to it.

Two properties align items. `justify-content` distributes free space along the main axis, with values such as `flex-start`, `center` and `space-between`. `align-items` positions items along the cross axis; `align-items: center` is the shortest way to centre an element vertically inside its parent.

Each item can grow and shrink. The shorthand `flex: 1` lets an item take an equal share of the spare space, so three items with `flex: 1` split a row into thirds. An item with `flex: 0 0 200px` stays exactly two hundred pixels wide whatever the container does.

By default all items stay on one line and shrink to fit. Setting `flex-wrap: wrap` lets them move onto new lines instead, which is how a row of cards becomes a grid on a wide screen and a single column on a phone. For layouts that need both rows and columns at once, CSS grid is usually the better tool.
title: Laying out a page with CSS flexbox

text:
# Working with Git branches

A branch in Git is a movable pointer to a commit. Creating one is cheap, so the usual practice is to start a new branch for every feature or fix and to keep the main branch in a releasable state.

`git switch -c feature/login` creates a branch called `feature/login` from the current commit and moves you onto it. New commits advance only the branch you are on. `git branch` lists local branches and marks the current one with an asterisk.

When the work is finished, you bring it back into the main branch. A merge, with `git merge feature/login` run while on `main`, creates a merge commit that has both histories as parents. A rebase, with `git rebase main` run on the feature branch, replays your commits on top of the latest `main` instead, which gives a straight line of history but rewrites the commits on the branch.

Conflicts happen when both branches changed the same lines. Git stops, marks the conflicting sections in the files, and waits for you to edit them, stage the result with `git add` and continue. Small, frequent merges keep conflicts small.

To share a branch, push it to the remote with `git push -u origin feature/login`; the `-u` flag records the remote branch as its upstream, so later pushes need no arguments. After the branch is merged, delete it locally with `git branch -d` and on the remote, so the list of branches stays short and meaningful.
title: Working with Git branches

text:
# Baking a lemon drizzle cake

A lemon drizzle cake is a simple loaf sponge soaked with lemon syrup while it is still warm. It keeps well for several days in a tin and needs no icing or decoration.

Heat the oven to 180 degrees, or 160 for a fan oven, and line a two-pound loaf tin with baking paper. Beat 225 grams of soft butter with 225 grams of caster sugar until the mixture is pale and fluffy, which takes about three minutes with an electric whisk.

Add four eggs one at a time, beating well after each, then fold in 225 grams of self-raising flour and the finely grated zest of one lemon. Fold gently with a large metal spoon so that the air you have beaten in stays in the batter.

Spoon the batter into the tin, level the top and bake for 45 to 50 minutes, until a skewer pushed into the centre comes out clean. If the top browns too quickly, cover it loosely with foil for the last ten minutes.

While the cake bakes, stir the juice of one and a half lemons into 85 grams of caster sugar. As soon as the cake comes out of the oven, prick it all over with a fork and pour the drizzle over the top. The juice sinks into the sponge and the sugar sets into a thin, crunchy crust as the cake cools in its tin. Lift it out only when it is completely cold, then slice and serve with tea.
title: Baking a lemon drizzle cake

text:
# Identifying garden birds in winter

Winter is a good season for learning garden birds. The trees are bare, birds come closer to feeders as natural food runs short, and the number of species visiting a garden is small enough to learn one at a time.

Start with size and shape before colour. A robin is round and upright with thin legs, a blackbird is larger with a long tail, and a wood pigeon is bigger again with a small head on a heavy body. Shape stays the same in poor light, when colours are hard to see.

Then look at behaviour. Blue tits and great tits hang upside down on seed feeders and dart away with a single seed. Dunnocks shuffle along the ground under bushes, picking at crumbs, and are easily mistaken for sparrows until you notice their thin beak. Starlings arrive in noisy groups and walk rather than hop.

Song helps too. Robins sing all winter to defend their territories, a thin, wistful warble that often starts before dawn. The wren, one of the smallest birds in the garden, has a surprisingly loud song that ends in a fast trill.

Keep a notebook by the window and write down the date, the species and the number you see at once. Over a few weeks you will notice patterns: which birds come early, which prefer the ground, and which disappear when a cat walks across the lawn.
title: Identifying garden birds in winter

text:
# Adjusting bicycle rim brakes

Rim brakes slow the bicycle by pressing rubber pads against the side of the wheel rim. As the pads wear and the cable stretches, the lever travels further before the brakes bite, so they need adjusting every few months.

First check the pads. Each pad should meet the rim squarely, sit entirely on the braking surface and never touch the tyre. A pad that has worn down to the grooves, or that has hardened and gone shiny, should be replaced rather than adjusted. Loosen the pad bolt, position the pad, and tighten it again while holding the pad in place.

To take up slack, turn the barrel adjuster where the cable enters the brake or the lever. Turning it out, anticlockwise, shortens the effective cable length and brings the pads closer to the rim. Two or three turns are usually enough. If the adjuster runs out of thread, screw it back in, loosen the cable clamp bolt, pull a little cable through and tighten the bolt again.

If one pad touches the rim while the other stands off, centre the brake. Most side-pull and dual-pivot brakes have a small centring screw on top; a quarter turn moves both arms noticeably.

Finish by squeezing the lever hard a dozen times to settle the cable, then check that the wheel spins freely and that the lever stops well before it reaches the handlebar.
title: Adjusting bicycle rim brakes

text:
# Setting up a home Wi-Fi network

A home wireless network usually consists of a single router supplied by the internet provider, sometimes extended with additional access points. A few settings make a large difference to its speed and security.

Place the router in a central, open position, away from thick walls, metal cabinets and microwave ovens. Wireless signals weaken quickly through brick and concrete, so a router hidden in a cupboard at one end of the house leaves distant rooms with a poor connection.

Sign in to the router's administration page with the address and password printed on its label, and change the administrator password straight away. Then give the network a name that does not identify your household and choose WPA3 encryption, or WPA2 if some of your devices are older. Use a long passphrase of several unrelated words.

Most routers broadcast on two frequency bands. The 2.4 GHz band reaches further but is slower and more crowded; the 5 GHz band is faster over short distances. Many routers can offer both under one network name and steer each device to the better band automatically.

For a large house, a mesh system of two or three units gives more even coverage than a single powerful router. Finally, turn on automatic firmware updates, so security fixes are installed without anyone having to remember them, and set up a separate guest network for visitors and smart devices.
title: Setting up a home Wi-Fi network

text:
# Typesetting a report with LaTeX

LaTeX is a typesetting system that turns a plain-text source file into a finished document, usually a PDF. You describe the structure of the text with commands, and LaTeX decides line breaks, page breaks, spacing and numbering.

Every document begins with `\documentclass`, which chooses the overall design: `article` for short papers, `report` for longer documents with chapters, and `book` for printed books. Packages loaded with `\usepackage` add features, such as `graphicx` for images or `amsmath` for advanced mathematics.

The text itself sits between `\begin{document}` and `\end{document}`. Commands such as `\section` and `\subsection` create numbered headings, and `\tableofcontents` collects them into a contents page on the next run. Paragraphs are separated by a blank line in the source; extra spaces and single line breaks are ignored.

Figures and tables are floats: LaTeX places them where they fit best rather than exactly where they appear in the source. Give each one a `\caption` and a `\label`, and refer to it with `\ref`, so the number in the text is always correct even after figures move.

Bibliographies are handled by a separate tool. You keep references in a `.bib` file, cite them in the text with `\cite`, and the bibliography is generated in a consistent style. Because cross-references and citations are resolved over several passes, a document is normally compiled two or three times before the final PDF is complete.
title: Typesetting a report with LaTeX
